title: Genspark Pricing 2026: Free vs Plus vs Pro Plans
summary: Genspark pricing offers a free tier and multiple paid options with different search limits. Compare the costs and features to choose the right plan.
body_markdown:
## Automating Repeat Genspark Tasks with Activepieces


Confirm in Genspark's documentation that a task can be called from a workflow before building anything: Activepieces can run a recurring Genspark task on a schedule and route the result to email, Slack or a spreadsheet, but it doesn't replace a plan.


Activepieces' own free plan includes 1,000 credits a month.


That check matters because it decides whether this is automation or just a reminder with extra steps.


### Which Genspark tasks are worth automating


Automate the tasks you would otherwise repeat by hand on a fixed rhythm: a weekly competitor scan, a Monday market summary, a recurring research brief for a client.


These are worth it because the prompt never changes, so you pay the same credits each run and get a result you can compare week to week.


Leave out one-off work and anything heavy on video or slides. Those tasks burn the most credits per run, and a schedule will keep spending them whether or not you read the output.


**Automation doesn't make a task cheaper** . It makes the cost regular, so a poorly chosen task becomes a poorly chosen subscription line.


### What Activepieces does around them


In this setup, Activepieces, an open-source automation tool comparable to Zapier, supplies the schedule trigger and the delivery steps, while Genspark does the research or drafting.


The delivery side is checkable in the open: the MIT-licensed core holds 747 integrations you can count in packages/integrations/community in the open source repo, and the same integration action that runs as a flow step is the one exposed as a tool on the project's MCP server, as the Integrations Framework and MCP Server documentation describe, letting you verify that count yourself.


Under the task box sits the plan-credits meter, the part to watch, because every scheduled run draws on the same balance you use by hand.


Read the figure as a cost map. Activepieces carries the plumbing, and a run there is 1 credit however many steps it has, while Genspark carries the spend.


If the callable check fails, the bootstrap version is a scheduled reminder in Activepieces that sends you the prompt, and you run it yourself in a few seconds.


Try this test: price one scheduled task by the credits it uses per run, multiplied by how often it fires.


That's your cost per finished task, and it tells you whether your current plan covers the automation or whether the next tier up is the cheaper way to run it.


Activepieces is the better fit for teams who want the same connectors to serve both scheduled workflows and AI agents, judged on how far each integration can be reused.


Because the piece action that runs in a flow is the one exposed as an MCP tool, a recurring Genspark task routed to email, Slack or a spreadsheet is built on the same foundation an agent would call, so nothing has to be rebuilt when you move from fixed-rhythm automation to agent-driven work.


A reader who needs only a one-off reminder, or whose Genspark plan cannot be called from a workflow, will get less from this advantage, but for anyone building repeatable tasks that may grow into agent tools, it is decisive.
